title: Lamentations 4:11–16
context: Lamentations 4:11–16 continues the poet’s lament. The LORD has accomplished his wrath and kindled a fire in Zion that consumed its foundations. The kings and peoples of the earth did not believe an enemy could enter Jerusalem’s gates. The poet names the reason: the sins of the prophets and the iniquities of the priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in the city. Now they wander like blind men, defiled with blood, and people drive them away crying “Unclean!” until even the nations say they cannot stay. The LORD’s anger has scattered them, and the leaders were shown no honor. Both traditions read the unit as confessing that judgment came through the failure of those who should have led the people in truth, a charge Jeremiah also makes (compare Jeremiah 5:31 and 23:11).

verses.text: The LORD has accomplished his wrath. He has poured out his fierce anger. He has kindled a fire in Zion, which has devoured its foundations.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says the LORD has accomplished his wrath, poured out his fierce anger, and kindled a fire that devoured Zion’s foundations. Arminian readers see God’s judgment as the just result of long-standing rebellion, which he warned about for generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign hand in the city’s destruction. Both traditions hold this as shared ground about divine wrath, and they read the verse as the poet’s confession that the disaster was the LORD’s judgment.

verses.text: The kings of the earth didn’t believe, neither did all the inhabitants of the world, that the adversary and the enemy would enter into the gates of Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says the kings and inhabitants of the earth did not believe an enemy could enter Jerusalem’s gates. Arminians see the shock of the city’s fall, since Jerusalem had seemed secure as the city of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as exposing false confidence in Zion’s safety. Both traditions note that Jeremiah warned against trusting the temple as a guarantee (Jeremiah 7:4), and they read the verse in that light.

verses.text: It is because of the sins of her prophets and the iniquities of her priests, that have shed the blood of the just in the middle of her.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says this happened because of the sins of the prophets and priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in the city. Arminian readers see leaders bearing special responsibility for leading the people astray.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as confessing the corruption of religious leadership. Both traditions compare Jeremiah’s charges against prophets and priests (Jeremiah 5:31 and 23:11), and they hold leaders accountable for the harm they caused.

verses.text: They wander as blind men in the streets. They are polluted with blood, So that men can’t touch their garments.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says the prophets and priests wander like blind men, defiled with blood, so that no one can touch their garments. Arminians see the irony of religious leaders becoming unclean, unable to serve as they once claimed to.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see their defilement as the result of their sin. Both traditions read the image of blindness as both literal confusion and spiritual failure, and they treat the verse as part of the poet’s indictment.

verses.text: “Go away!” they cried to them. “Unclean! Go away! Go away! Don’t touch! When they fled away and wandered, men said among the nations, “They can’t live here any more.”
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says people cried to them, “Unclean! Go away! Don’t touch!” and even among the nations they were told they could not stay. Arminian readers see the leaders treated as lepers once were (compare Leviticus 13:45), a striking reversal for priests and prophets.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the shame that came on those who led the people astray. Both traditions read the verse as showing that their sin brought rejection both at home and abroad.

verses.text: The LORD’s anger has scattered them. He will not pay attention to them any more. They didn’t respect the persons of the priests. They didn’t favor the elders.
verses.arminianNotes: The poet says the LORD’s anger has scattered them and he will no longer regard them, since they did not honor priests or elders. Arminians see God’s judgment on leaders who failed, which removed them from their place of honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign hand in scattering them. Both traditions note that the last line may describe the enemy’s treatment of the leaders, and they hold that reading open.
